children: U.S. stocks slid as rising inflation bolstered the case for another rate increase this year.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average slid 48.62 points, or 0.09%, to 51621.48. The S&P 500 dropped 86.51 points, or 1.11%, to 7718.94 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite lost 511.51 points, or 1.88%, to 26692.87.
The Russell 2000 index of small-cap stocks declined almost 2%, entering correction territory as it is more than 10% below record highs earlier this year.

Bond yields rose sharply following a hot inflation report, but generally declined later in the session as chip and AI stocks slipped. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note declined 0.027 percentage point to 5.189%, its lowest level in nearly three weeks. The yield on the two-year Treasury rose 0.008 percentage point to 4.800%. The 30-year bond yield declined 0.038 percentage point to 5.524%.
The dollar strengthened on the inflation news, with the ICE dollar index rising 0.38% to its highest level in over a year. Gold futures lost 1.64% to $4084.80 per troy ounce.

Brent crude rose 0.4% to $106.06 a barrel. Tensions in the Middle East remained elevated after Houthi militants struck a building at Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil producer, following an attack on the international airport in the capital this past weekend.

Inflation rose in September with consumer prices up 3.7% compared with the same period a year earlier. Economists polled by the Wall Street Journal had expected a 3.6% increase. It was a bigger jump than the 3.4% gain in August, a sign that high energy prices are continuing to weigh heavily on consumers ahead of midterm elections.
Energy costs drove inflation, with gas prices up 9.1% from the prior month and 34% in the past year. Excluding energy and food costs, core inflation also topped economists' projections, rising 2.6%.

Higher-than-expected inflation will increase pressure on the Federal Reserve to consider raising interest rates again. While many were expecting the Fed to hold off until December, some analysts now think a rate hike could happen this month.

"Coming into today, the argument for holding in October rested on inflation staying mostly contained to energy," Jason Pride, chief of investment strategy and research at Glenmede, said in a note. "Price pressure appeared to be showing up in most corners of the consumption basket at once."

The prospect of higher rates is weighing on the country's biggest banks, which are reporting third-quarter results this week. Morgan Stanley's shares closed down 2.75%, despite the bank posting higher profit and beating Wall Street estimates.

Bank of America's stock slipped 4.8% after third-quarter profit missed analysts' forecasts. That miss took into account a $1.2 billion fine the bank was slapped with by the Treasury Department after regulators found it had insufficient systems to monitor and report financial crimes.

The AI sector slumped with Oracle, Marvell Technology and cloud-computing firm CoreWeave among the biggest losers. Rising Treasury yields are creating concerns about AI companies' immense ambitions for debt-funded spending. The PHLX Semiconductor Index has declined for six consecutive days, its longest losing streak in more than a year.
Shares of Apple bucked the downtrend in technology rising 0.5%. That gain helped Apple become the second company to close with a market cap above $5 trillion, following Nvidia.

Netflix is cutting 6% of its staff, or roughly 1,000 workers, biggest round of layoffs since 2022. The streaming platform has struggled to maintain growth and customer engagement as it faces increasing competition from YouTube and other streamers.
